title: Stop Paying the Job-Loyalty Penalty
meta_description: Measure total compensation, benchmark your role, test the market, negotiate with evidence and compare offers without sacrificing career stability.

sections.heading: Loyalty Is a Value, Not a Compensation Method
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows an exhausted employee facing a laptop and work papers because a loyalty penalty is rarely announced. It accumulates when responsibilities, market pay and living costs move faster than salary while the employee keeps delivering. The problem is not staying itself. The problem is staying without measuring what the exchange has become.

Long tenure can create skill, trust, flexibility, strong colleagues and meaningful work. Those are real benefits. It can also create information asymmetry: the employer knows the person’s current pay, while the employee stops testing what another organization would pay for the same capability. A fair decision puts both sides of that ledger in writing.

Do not begin with the claim that every job switch produces a raise. Labour markets vary by occupation, geography, cycle, seniority and individual performance. Switching can reduce pay or stability. Use [[S1|employee-tenure evidence]], current wage data and actual opportunities to estimate the trade rather than repeating a viral percentage.

Define the possible penalty broadly. It may include base salary, bonus target, overtime, equity, pension or retirement match, health coverage, paid leave, flexibility, commute, learning, promotion path and workload. A higher salary paired with weak insurance, uncertain bonus and a long commute may not improve household finances.

Separate gratitude from pricing. An employer that trained someone early deserves professional effort and honest notice; it does not acquire permanent rights to discounted labour. Likewise, an employee who values a supportive manager can rationally accept less cash, provided the size of that choice is known and affordable.

Build a decision cadence before resentment. Review role scope and total compensation at least annually and after promotions, reorganizations, certifications or major market shifts. A scheduled review prevents every difficult week from becoming a resignation trigger and prevents five quiet years from passing without a market check.

The objective is not maximum pay at any cost. It is an informed agreement: current compensation is understood, external value is tested, noncash benefits are priced, risks are funded and the employee chooses to stay, negotiate or move. Loyalty becomes healthier when it is renewed rather than assumed.

sections.heading: Build a Total-Compensation Ledger
paragraphs: Start with the last twelve months. Record gross base pay, overtime, shift premiums, commission, cash bonus, equity that vested, employer retirement contributions, health premiums paid by the employer and other recurring benefits. Use payslips, plan documents and award statements. Do not value a discretionary bonus at its headline maximum.

Convert benefits into comparable annual amounts without pretending every dollar has equal utility. Employer insurance cost is not automatically what the employee would pay personally, and unused perks are not compensation merely because a brochure lists them. Show employer cost, personal value and replacement cost in separate columns.

Value paid time off using usable days, not nominal policy. Include holidays, vacation, sick leave, parental leave and the culture around taking them. A role offering unlimited leave may deliver less actual time than one with a fixed balance. Review how leave affects burnout, childcare and travel rather than only multiplying days by salary.

Record flexibility with evidence: remote days actually used, schedule control, travel frequency, after-hours expectations and commute cost. Price fuel, fares, parking, meals, clothing and unpaid commute hours. Flexibility can be worth substantial money, but it should not excuse unlimited work or hidden availability.

For equity, distinguish grant value, current value, vesting, exercise cost, tax and concentration. Unvested awards are conditional retention incentives, not money already earned. Model outcomes if the company value falls, an acquisition changes terms or departure occurs before vesting. Never use a single optimistic valuation.

Add career capital: funded education, portfolio-quality projects, access to decision-makers, leadership scope and portable credentials. Give each a time horizon and evidence. “Good exposure” has little value if the role repeats familiar work and no promotion criteria exist. Learning should result in a stronger external or internal opportunity.

Finish with after-tax household impact. A compensation package matters through cash available, benefits replaced and risk absorbed. Keep the ledger dated, with source documents and assumptions. It becomes the baseline for an internal raise request and the comparison sheet for any outside offer.

sections.heading: Measure the Role You Actually Perform
paragraphs: Job titles often lag duties. List recurring decisions, people led, budget controlled, revenue influenced, systems owned, risk carried and problems solved. Compare the current work with the original description and with higher-level roles inside the organization. Scope evidence is stronger than saying the workload feels larger.

Create an achievement inventory using problem, action and result. Quantify money saved, revenue supported, cycle time reduced, quality improved, incidents prevented, clients retained or people developed. Where a dollar figure would be speculative, use verifiable operational measures. Keep confidential information out of personal files.

Separate team outcomes from personal contribution. Credit collaborators and state the part personally owned. Exaggerated claims can damage credibility in both internal reviews and interviews. The aim is to make invisible work visible without converting shared success into a private trophy.

Identify work performed above level and work that merely accumulated. More tasks do not automatically justify higher pay if they are routine or temporary. Higher autonomy, complexity, consequence and organizational reach are more persuasive. Ask whether the role would be advertised differently if the employer had to replace it today.

Map skills to external language. Internal systems and acronyms can conceal portable ability. Translate “owns weekly XQ process” into vendor management, financial control, data quality, stakeholder communication or another recognized competency. Verify the translation against real job descriptions, not invented keywords.

Record constraints too. A title may look senior while authority, staffing or budget remains junior. A prestigious employer may narrow experience. If the role cannot provide the next skill, state what is missing and a deadline to obtain it through a project, training or move.

Update a private master résumé quarterly. It is not a job application; it is an evidence archive. Add outcomes while documents and context exist. Regular maintenance reduces panic when a recruiter calls or reorganization arrives, and it makes compensation conversations specific.

sections.heading: Benchmark the Market With More Than a Salary Website
paragraphs: Use several sources: official occupational wage data, reputable salary surveys, recruiter ranges, transparent job postings and actual interviews. Each source has bias. Self-reported sites can mix levels; postings may show wide legal ranges; recruiters may emphasize openings they control; national medians can ignore city and specialty.

Define the benchmark role before collecting numbers. Match function, level, industry, organization size, geography, remote status, management scope and scarce skills. A software title at a start-up may not match the same title at a regulated multinational. Avoid choosing only comparisons that support a desired conclusion.

Use [[S2|occupational wage data]] as an anchor and [[S3|wage-growth evidence]] for context, then adjust with current local openings. Record collection dates. A boom-era offer from years ago is not current market evidence, and a temporary hiring freeze is not proof that long-term value disappeared.

Compare percentiles carefully. Someone new to a level may reasonably sit below the midpoint while an experienced high performer may target higher. A salary range does not guarantee placement. Ask what experience, results and scope explain the chosen position rather than treating the top as an entitlement.

Test demand by counting credible openings and required qualifications, not recruiter messages alone. Distinguish active roles from duplicated listings and evergreen talent pools. Note interview conversion: applications to screens, screens to final rounds and finals to offers. Market value becomes clearer through repeated real responses.

Adjust for total compensation. Add typical bonus, equity, retirement contributions, health cost, leave and flexibility. If data are weak, show a range. Never compare current total pay with only an advertised base or compare an outside maximum with the current guaranteed amount.

Calculate the cost of a persistent gap. Apply a conservative annual difference to several years, then include likely percentage raises, employer retirement contributions and bonus effects. Do not present the result as guaranteed lost wealth; use it to show why a small recurring base gap can matter more than one missed bonus. Discount uncertain years and disclose assumptions.

Check internal comparators carefully. Pay transparency may reveal ranges or peers, but experience, location, performance and hire date can explain some differences. Use lawful information and protect colleague privacy. The strongest question is whether the organization can explain placement through consistent factors, not whether every person has identical pay.

Write a market conclusion with confidence level: “Comparable base appears 8–15 percent higher, supported by three local postings, one recruiter range and two interviews.” That is actionable. “The internet says I am underpaid” is not. Preserve evidence for a calm internal conversation.

sections.heading: Run Interviews as a Market Test
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a recruiter reviewing a candidate’s documents across a table. It represents an external market test, not a threat. Interviews reveal how employers describe the role, which skills receive attention, what compensation is budgeted and whether the employee’s evidence persuades strangers outside the current company.

Prepare before applying. Update résumé, professional profile, work samples where permitted and accomplishment stories. Choose target roles with plausible fit. A scattershot campaign creates noisy rejection data and can expose confidential intentions. Use personal devices, personal contact details and personal time.

Ask compensation questions at the appropriate stage. Seek the budgeted base range, bonus mechanics, equity terms, benefits, location expectations and hiring timeline. Do not disclose unnecessary current salary where law or strategy permits declining. State the target based on role value and total package.

Treat interview performance as a skill. A weak first round may reflect preparation, not market value. Review which examples failed, whether technical knowledge is current and whether the target level matches demonstrated scope. Improve the signal before concluding that the present salary is fair.

Verify opportunity quality. Ask why the role is open, how success is measured, manager tenure, team turnover, workload, decision authority and financial outlook. Speak with future colleagues when possible. A company eager to pay more may be pricing instability or unreasonable expectations.

Keep a search log containing role, date, range, stage, feedback and concerns. Do not store employer confidential material. After several credible processes, patterns emerge: recurring skill gaps, compensation bands and role differences. One unusually high or low offer should not define the market.

An interview does not obligate departure. It creates evidence and optionality. Conduct the process honestly; do not solicit an offer solely as a bluff if there is no circumstance under which it could be accepted. Reputation and other people’s time are part of the decision.

sections.heading: Ask for an Internal Correction With Evidence
paragraphs: Choose the request: market adjustment, promotion, retention adjustment, bonus, equity refresh, title correction, development plan or some combination. A vague request for “more” is easy to defer. Tie the request to current scope, documented results, market evidence and the employer’s compensation cycle.

Schedule a dedicated conversation rather than adding pay in the final minute of a status meeting. Share a concise case in advance if culture permits. Begin with commitment to the role and facts, not accusations about loyalty. State the requested range and effective timing clearly.

Use evidence the manager can carry upward: expanded responsibilities, measurable outcomes, replacement-market data and internal level alignment. Avoid personal bills as the main rationale. Living costs matter to the employee, but compensation decisions are more likely to move through role value, performance and retention risk.

Ask about process and authority. The manager may support the case but lack budget. Learn who decides, which documentation is required, when committees meet and what alternatives exist. A sympathetic conversation without owner, date or next step is not a plan.

If the answer is “not now,” request written milestones and a review date. Define what level, outcomes or business condition would support change. Beware goals that expand indefinitely. Reassess if the employer asks for higher-level work without title, pay or a credible timeline.

Consider noncash improvements only at fair value. Additional leave, remote work, training, schedule control or reduced travel may solve real needs. Do not accept a cheap perk as equivalent to recurring base pay unless it genuinely is. Base salary often affects future raises, bonus, retirement contributions and outside negotiations.

Prepare for objections without turning the meeting adversarial. Budget limits, pay equity, cycle timing and performance calibration can be legitimate constraints. Ask which constraint applies and what evidence could change it. Distinguish “cannot this quarter” from “will not price this role differently.” The distinction informs whether patience or a search is rational.

Do not make a resignation threat unless prepared to resign. A deadline invented to force action can damage trust and leave the employee exposed if the employer accepts it. Instead, state the decision window created by real circumstances, such as an external written offer, and remain truthful about timing.

Document the outcome professionally. Confirm agreed amount, title, responsibilities, effective date and any conditions through official channels. Do not celebrate a verbal promise as completed compensation. Check the first payslip or award statement and correct discrepancies promptly.

sections.heading: Price Benefits, Vesting and Switching Costs
paragraphs: An outside offer must clear the switching-cost hurdle. List forfeited bonus, unvested equity, pension vesting, accrued leave, health deductibles, commuter changes, relocation, probation risk and unpaid gap. Put timing beside each amount. A signing bonus may offset some losses but often has repayment conditions.

Read the offer and plan documents. Bonus “target” may be discretionary; equity may use an uncertain valuation; employer retirement contributions may require service; insurance networks may exclude current clinicians. Ask for summaries and effective dates before accepting, not after resigning.

Model cash flow for the first year and a normal later year. The first year can contain signing bonus, partial bonus, benefit waiting periods and duplicate deductibles. Later years reveal recurring economics. Compare conservative, expected and upside cases rather than only the recruiter’s illustration.

Value remote and hybrid terms through written policy and team practice. A company-wide policy can change, while a contractual arrangement may offer more protection. Ask how often the team attends, who approves exceptions and whether location affects pay. Avoid paying relocation costs based on an informal promise.

Assess employment stability without pretending certainty. Review funding, profitability where available, customer concentration, recent layoffs, leadership changes and role necessity. A higher salary in a fragile role may still be rational if the emergency fund and career options are strong; the risk must be explicit.

Include household effects: partner employment, childcare, elder care, school, commute and health treatment. A change that works on an individual spreadsheet may fail operationally. Discuss timing and contingency with affected people before signing.

Set a required premium or strategic gain. Someone leaving a safe, flexible role may require substantial compensation; someone moving into a high-growth skill area may accept a smaller immediate increase. The hurdle should reflect actual risk and goals, not a universal switching percentage.

sections.heading: Treat Counteroffers as a New Contract Decision
paragraphs: A counteroffer can correct pay quickly, preserve relationships and avoid transition. It can also address only salary while leaving scope, promotion, trust or workload unchanged. Revisit the reasons for searching and score each one. If compensation was not the only issue, a matching number may not solve the decision.

Ask why the correction required a resignation. Sometimes budgets truly move only under retention pressure; sometimes the company had incomplete market information. The answer matters less than the durability of the remedy. Obtain written amount, title, reporting line, duties and effective date.

Consider how the employer will view retention risk, but avoid simplistic claims that everyone accepting a counteroffer is fired. Outcomes vary. Ask whether succession, project access or advancement could change. Judge the specific organization and manager rather than folklore.

Do not reveal the outside offer document unless necessary and permitted. You can state verified terms without sharing another employer’s confidential material. Never invent an offer. A fabricated negotiation can destroy trust and may have legal or disciplinary consequences.

Compare both opportunities fresh. The external employer may improve its package; the current employer may offer a broader role. Use the same total-compensation and risk sheet. Do not let familiarity automatically win, and do not let the excitement of being wanted erase due diligence.

Set a short, respectful decision timeline consistent with both parties’ needs. Avoid running repeated auctions after a fair agreement. Negotiation should improve fit, not maximize pressure until relationships break.

If staying, reset expectations and withdraw from the outside process promptly. If leaving, decline the counteroffer professionally. Preserve records and commitments either way. The decision is a contract and career choice, not a referendum on personal loyalty.

sections.heading: Negotiate an Outside Offer Without Losing It
paragraphs: Wait for a written offer or clear verbal terms before negotiating. Express enthusiasm, ask for the complete package and request reasonable review time. Identify the two or three terms with greatest value rather than reopening every line. A focused request is easier to approve.

Anchor the request in role scope, market evidence, competing verified terms and switching costs. State a specific base or range, not “Can you do better?” If base is constrained, consider signing bonus, start date, equity, leave, remote terms, review timing, title or professional development.

The late photograph shows professionals reviewing documents together because negotiation ends in paperwork. Read salary, bonus definition, equity instrument, vesting, benefits, probation, notice, restrictive covenants, intellectual-property terms and contingencies. Ask qualified counsel about clauses you do not understand.

Do not resign until material contingencies are understood. Background checks, references, work authorization and approvals can delay or cancel a start. Decide how much confirmation is needed for the risk, and retain an emergency fund. No offer is risk-free until work begins, and employment may remain terminable.

Avoid negotiating through false claims. Do not inflate current pay, invent competing offers or misrepresent deadlines. You can protect privacy and still be truthful. Long-term earning power depends partly on reputation.

Confirm every agreed change in the final written offer. Recruiter emails and calls may not amend the contract. Compare the final document with the negotiation log and ask about discrepancies before signing. Save a copy outside the employer’s system.

Calculate the minimum acceptable outcome before the call. Include current package, switching costs, risk premium and the strategic value of the new scope. Decide which terms are essential and which can trade. Precommitment prevents a polished recruiter from turning excitement into acceptance below the household’s real threshold.

Review tax and cash timing without offering personal tax advice to yourself from a recruiter estimate. Bonus withholding, equity taxation, benefit deductions and relocation reimbursement can differ from headline values. Ask for plan documents and use a qualified adviser where material. A higher gross offer can produce uneven first-year cash.

Once accepted, stop interviewing unless a serious issue emerges. Notify other employers courteously. Prepare references, handover and household cash for the transition. The goal is not merely to win the offer; it is to enter the new role with trust and financial stability.

sections.heading: Leave Without Burning Career Capital
paragraphs: Check notice obligations, bonus dates, equity vesting, leave payout, benefit termination and restrictive covenants before resigning. Do not remove confidential files, customer lists, code or proprietary work. Build a personal record only from information you are entitled to retain, such as payslips and benefit statements.

Resign directly and briefly after the new decision is firm. Thank the employer, state the final working date and offer a practical handover. Avoid unloading every grievance in the resignation letter. Specific constructive feedback can be shared through appropriate channels if it is safe and useful.

Create a transition inventory of projects, owners, deadlines, risks and documentation. Train successors within reasonable limits. A strong handover protects colleagues and references, but it does not require unpaid availability forever. Agree the boundary for post-departure questions.

Secure household administration: health coverage, retirement rollover or preservation, final pay, tax forms, expense reimbursement and contact details. Do not rush a retirement-account transfer without comparing fees, investments, creditor rules and tax treatment. Confirm final payments against statements.

Preserve relationships individually. Thank mentors, peers and direct reports; connect through personal professional channels where appropriate. Do not recruit colleagues improperly or use departure to spread confidential information. A career network compounds like any other asset.

Expect emotional ambiguity. Leaving a good team can feel disloyal even when the decision is rational. Staying after a fair internal correction can feel anticlimactic. Use the written decision criteria rather than interpreting discomfort as proof of error.

Review the transition after ninety days. Compare promised role, workload, flexibility and compensation with reality. Update the career ledger and emergency plan. Early evidence helps address mismatches before they become another long period of unmeasured loyalty.

sections.heading: Know When Staying Is the Higher-Value Choice
paragraphs: Staying can be financially superior when pay is fair, benefits are unusually strong, flexibility solves expensive constraints and the role builds scarce skills. It can also be wise during a fragile household period when transition risk is unaffordable. The decision should come from measured value, not fear of interviewing.

A strong manager can accelerate a career more than a modest immediate raise. Evaluate sponsorship, feedback quality, project access and promotion history. Ask whether the manager has delivered prior commitments. Good intentions without organizational influence may not produce advancement.

Model a two-year stay case with specific outcomes: compensation adjustment, title, project, credential, team responsibility and review dates. If the plan depends on vague future recognition, reduce confidence. Set an exit trigger if essential milestones do not occur.

Consider skill half-life. A comfortable role can become risky if tools, regulation or customer needs change while the work stays static. Reserve time for current learning and external relationships. Staying should not mean becoming unemployable outside one company’s systems.

Use internal mobility. Another team may correct scope, pay and growth without losing benefits or tenure. Apply the same diligence as an external move: manager, expectations, range, transition and written terms. Internal familiarity can hide role risk as easily as external excitement can.

Maintain external readiness even when satisfied. Keep résumé evidence, professional contacts, emergency savings and credentials current. This is not disloyal; it protects the household from layoffs, illness, mergers and leadership changes. Optionality supports a calmer relationship with the employer.

Write the reason for staying in one paragraph and assign a review date. “This role is worth an estimated $X less in cash because it saves Y commute hours, preserves Z benefit and delivers a defined promotion project by September” is a choice. “It is easier” is not enough.

sections.heading: Run an Annual Career Pricing Review
paragraphs: Choose a month away from crisis and compensation deadlines. Update the total-compensation ledger, role scope, achievements, market evidence, skill gaps and household constraints. Review every time duties change materially, not only after a disappointing raise.

Track salary progression in real and nominal terms, but do not use inflation as the sole argument. Compare purchasing power, market movement, internal scope and total package. A nominal raise can still be a market decline; a flat salary with a valuable schedule change may still improve life.

Maintain three plans: stay and grow, negotiate, and search. Each needs next actions, evidence and a date. Having all three prevents an unsuccessful raise request from becoming panic and prevents a pleasant review from ending external awareness.

Audit pay equity and discrimination concerns carefully. Use [[S7|official equal-pay resources]], internal channels and qualified legal advice where appropriate. Preserve factual records. A market negotiation framework does not replace rights or remedies when compensation differences involve unlawful discrimination.

Check financial readiness for a move: emergency fund, health transition, debt, relocation and possible income gap. Strong savings increase bargaining power because the employee can reject unsuitable terms. Do not resign impulsively as a negotiation tactic.

Share career decisions with affected household members while protecting employer confidentiality. Agree the acceptable commute, travel, schedule and risk. A higher offer that destabilizes care or health may not pass the household test.

Keep a decision journal. Record the evidence, assumptions, risks, household priorities and reason for the chosen path. Revisit it after six and twelve months. The journal distinguishes a flawed process from an unpredictable outcome and prevents hindsight from rewriting what was reasonably knowable.

Watch for nonfinancial warning signs that cannot be priced away: harassment, retaliation, unsafe practices, unethical instructions or serious health damage. Use appropriate internal, regulatory, legal or medical support. A compensation framework is not a reason to remain in harmful conditions while waiting for a better number.

The final measure is agency. The employee can stay with confidence, negotiate with evidence or move after due diligence. The loyalty penalty disappears not whenever someone quits, but whenever tenure is consciously repriced and the chosen exchange remains fair enough to renew.

summary: A job-loyalty penalty develops when responsibilities and market pay rise faster than compensation while an employee stops checking the exchange. Staying is not automatically a mistake. Long tenure can provide strong benefits, flexibility, relationships and career capital. The risk is staying without measuring their value or the opportunity cost.

Begin with a total-compensation ledger covering base pay, reliable bonus, vested equity, employer retirement contributions, health coverage, paid leave, flexibility, commute and career development. Separate employer cost from personal value. Model equity conservatively and identify vesting, tax and concentration risk.

Document the role actually performed. Record decisions, people, budget, revenue, systems, risk and measurable results. Translate internal language into portable skills. Compare expanded complexity and autonomy with the formal level; more routine tasks alone do not establish a higher-value role.

Benchmark through several sources: official wage data, reputable surveys, current postings, recruiter ranges and real interviews. Match geography, industry, organization size, level and management scope. Compare total packages rather than current total compensation with an advertised base maximum.

Interviews are an external market test. Use personal devices and time, target credible roles and keep a log of ranges, stages, feedback and concerns. Ask why the position is open, how success is measured and what workload and turnover look like. One offer does not define the market.

For an internal correction, request a specific market adjustment, promotion, title or development plan. Use scope, results and replacement-market evidence rather than personal bills. Ask who decides, what evidence is required and when the next decision occurs. Convert “not now” into written milestones and a review date.

Compare outside offers after benefits and switching costs. Include forfeited bonus, equity, pension vesting, insurance deductibles, relocation, probation risk and household effects. Model the first year and a normal later year. Require a premium or strategic gain that fits the actual risk.

A counteroffer is a new contract decision. Check whether it solves workload, management and progression as well as salary. Compare both opportunities with the same sheet and obtain every material term in writing. Never fabricate another offer or share confidential documents casually.

Negotiate an outside offer through role value, market evidence and verified switching costs. Focus on the terms that matter most. Read bonus, equity, benefits, restrictive covenants and contingencies. Do not resign before material approvals are understood, and maintain emergency cash for transition risk.

If leaving, protect career capital. Follow notice rules, preserve confidentiality, deliver a practical handover and reconcile final pay and benefits. If staying, define the compensation, skill and promotion outcomes that justify another period of tenure and set an exit trigger if they fail.

Price noncash value honestly. Paid leave, health coverage, retirement contributions, flexibility, commute and a strong manager can justify accepting less base pay, but only when those benefits are actually usable and durable. Show employer cost, personal value and replacement cost separately. Do not value unvested equity or a discretionary bonus as guaranteed cash.

Protect the household before acting. Maintain emergency savings, understand health and benefit transitions, check notice and restrictive terms, and discuss commute, care and relocation with affected people. A strong offer can still fail if first-year cash flow, probation risk or family logistics are ignored. Career optionality becomes more valuable when savings allow unsuitable terms to be rejected.

Use a decision journal containing evidence, assumptions, risks and the reason for staying, negotiating or moving. Revisit it after six and twelve months. This prevents hindsight from confusing a sound process with an unpredictable result and reveals whether promised scope, flexibility and compensation appeared in practice.

Review career pricing annually and after major scope changes. Maintain stay, negotiate and search plans, plus financial readiness for each. Success is not changing jobs repeatedly. It is having enough evidence and optionality to renew loyalty deliberately instead of paying for it unknowingly.

faq.question: Does changing jobs always increase pay?
faq.answer: No. Outcomes vary by occupation, cycle, level and person. Compare executable offers and total compensation rather than a general switching statistic.

faq.question: How often should I benchmark my salary?
faq.answer: Review annually and after major scope, title, skill or market changes. Frequent browsing is less useful than a dated evidence file.

faq.question: Should I tell my manager I am interviewing?
faq.answer: Usually not until there is a strategic reason and you understand the risk. An evidence-based pay discussion can occur without threats.

faq.question: Is a counteroffer always a bad idea?
faq.answer: No. Test whether written terms solve the original reasons for searching and whether the remedy is durable.

faq.question: How do I value remote work?
faq.answer: Estimate commute cost, time, care impact and schedule control, then consider policy durability. Do not assign an arbitrary universal amount.

faq.question: Should I share my current salary with a recruiter?
faq.answer: Requirements vary. Where lawful, you can redirect toward the role’s budget and your target without making false statements.

faq.question: What if I like my job but appear underpaid?
faq.answer: Quantify the gap, request an internal correction and explicitly value benefits and growth. Staying can be rational when the known trade-off is affordable.

glossary.definition: The compensation or career-value gap that can emerge when long-tenured workers are not repriced with their market and scope.
Base pay plus credible variable pay, equity, employer benefits and other measurable work value.
A pay correction intended to align compensation with external or internal market evidence.
An employer range associated with a role, level and location under its compensation structure.
The process by which conditional retirement or equity benefits become owned under plan terms.
A one-time payment for joining, often subject to tax and repayment conditions.
Revised terms from a current employer intended to retain an employee who may leave.
Portable skills, achievements, reputation and relationships that improve future opportunities.
Money, benefits, time, risk and household disruption incurred when changing roles.
Change in pay after accounting for inflation under a stated measure.
